item.title: Current-Dependent Meta-GGA and Local Hybrid Functionals for Relativistic NMR Shifts
item.description: arXiv:2611.31432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NMR chemical shifts are key for the characterization of novel compounds. Especially for molecules with heavy elements, the experimental data is often corroborated with computational studies in density functional theory (DFT). However, modern meta-generalized gradient approximations (meta-GGAs) and local hybrid functionals are not widely supported in relativistic calculations with quantum chemistry program suites. So far, their current-dependent generalization in the spirit of Dobson, Becke, and Tao was not presented at all. This generalization ensures gauge invariance and does not introduce artifacts--unlike the more popular field-dependent generalization of the kinetic-energy density. In non-relativistic and scalar-relativistic calculations, the first was shown to be superior but the current density only arises due to the magnetic field perturbation. In contrast, spin--orbit coupling also induces current densities in the preceding ground-state calculation and the DFT framework needs to be generalized to a current density functional theory (CDFT) for consistency with the current-dependent response equations. Herein, we present the two-component relativistic generalization of the current-dependent kinetic-energy density of a Kramers-restricted Kohn--Sham reference for meta-GGAs and local hybrid functionals in NMR calculations. The extension is invariant under a position-dependent phase and a position-dependent spin rotation of the spinors, or a local U(1)$\times$SU(2) transformation. Relativistic effects are considered with exact two-component theory using a superposition of atomic potentials to include the two-electron picture-change correction (SAP-X2C).
item.dc:creator: Yannick J. Franzke, Christof Holzer

item.title: Sum rules for the relativistic and retarded Bethe approximation in electron-neutral-atom collisions
item.description: arXiv:2611.31710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For high partial waves the reactance matrix for electron-atom collisions may be replaced by the Bethe approximation, and for optically allowed transitions the slowly convergent sum over partial waves can then be performed exactly by means of the sum rules of Burgess. For neutral targets the Bethe integrals and the sum rules take a particularly simple form in terms of Legendre functions of the second kind of a single argument $\chi=(k^2+k'^2)/2kk'$. We show that this structure survives in a fully relativistic description. For a projectile described by free Dirac waves interacting through the retarded M{\o}ller interaction, the Bethe integrals of every multipole order are obtained from the static ones by the replacement $\chi\to\chi_q=(k^2+k'^2-q^2)/2kk'$, where $q$ is the energy transfer divided by $c$. For dipole transitions we give closed-form sum rules over all partial waves above any $l_0\ge2$ for the Coulomb (charge-density) interaction, for the magnetic dipole interaction and for the long-range transverse electric interaction, including its interference with the Coulomb term. In each case the sum reduces to a quadratic form in $Q_{l_0-1}(\chi_q)$ and $Q_{l_0}(\chi_q)$ with coefficients rational in $l_0$. As the impact energy increases $\chi_q\to1$ and the partial-wave sums converge ever more slowly, so that the sum rules become most useful precisely in the relativistic regime.
item.dc:creator: Colm T. Whelan

item.title: OMNI-P3x universal neural network potential for large-scale computational photochemistry workflows
item.description: arXiv:2611.32133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational photochemistry supports the design and understanding of new materials. However, the high cost of excited-state quantum-mechanical (QM) calculations makes screening large molecular libraries prohibitively expensive. To address this limitation, we introduce OMNI-P3x, a universal machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) for singlet ground- and excited-state simulations of neutral and charged organic molecules. Trained on both ground- and excited-state conformations, it performs complete computational photochemistry workflows with accuracy approaching TD-DFT. We demonstrate its practical applicability by screening a combinatorial library of 234,375 flavylium derivatives, where the pretrained model performs ground-state geometry optimization and predicts absorption properties without additional QM calculations. Following fine-tuning, we further screen 162,960 xanthene-based dyes, identifying new candidates for red, near-infrared and short-wavelength infrared emission. Furthermore, state-dependent neural charges, learned without reference atomic charges, provide an interpretable picture of intramolecular charge redistribution upon excitation.
item.dc:creator: Miko{\l}aj Martyka, Joanna Jankowska, Pavlo O. Dral

item.title: Nonemissive Intermediates: Photon-Yield Limits and Timing Advantages for Optogenetic Light
item.description: arXiv:2611.32167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximizing photon yield need not minimize the excitation required for a brief optogenetic stimulus. We consider a reversible luminescent source in which a mechanically prepared excitation can reach the emitter directly or through one nonemissive intermediate. Dividing the mechanically prepared photon yield by the yield from direct optical excitation of the emitter gives the probability of successful arrival. When intermediate loss is positive, the same two yields predict the mean photoluminescence emission time given independently calibrated terminal rates and thermal weights. A separate optical decay trace can test this prediction. For a fixed budget of squared transfer couplings and allocation-independent terminal losses, we prove that either direct transfer or a pure relay attains the maximum total yield. Above a sharp threshold in the intermediate loss rate, direct transfer is globally optimal. In a spectrally weighted model of the light-gated channel Chrimson, a fixed relay in this regime emits 5.21% fewer photons per prepared excitation than direct transfer. Its earlier emission produces the same mean conductance over 20 ms with 16.54% less effective preparation and leaves lower residual conductance at 50 ms. Weak-drive response kernels show how early photons contribute to activation while leaving time for closure. Sustained stimulation can favor direct transfer again. Replaying calibrated emission waveforms with a common spectrum in voltage-clamped cells would test which source meets both conductance targets with fewer prepared excitations.
item.dc:creator: Jingqi Chen, Qiang Zhou, Yue Zhu, Xin Xu

item.title: Perturbation of CO A1{\Pi} by a3{\Pi} should have been undetectable: detection, mechanism, and surprises
item.description: arXiv:2611.32289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A direct perturbation between the $a^3\Pi$ and $A^1\Pi$ vibrational levels of two electronic states that belong to the same electronic configuration of the carbon monoxide molecule should be unobservably weak because the vibrational overlap integral $\langle a^3\Pi,v' \mid A^1\Pi,v'' \rangle$ for their near-degenerate levels is extremely small. Yet level-shift and transition-intensity signatures of the $a^3\Pi(v = 13) \sim A^1\Pi(v = 2)$ perturbation are unmistakably present in the $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O}$ isotopologue. A detailed study of, among others, the $A^1\Pi$ - $X^1\Sigma^+(2, 0)$, $B^1\Sigma^+$ - $A^1\Pi(0, 2)$, and $C^1\Sigma^+$ - $A^1\Pi(0, 2)$ spectra, obtained by the VUV- and Vis-FT complementary techniques in the energy regions of the six crossing points ($e$- and $f$-symmetry, $|\Omega| = 0, 1, 2$) between the $a^3\Pi(v = 13)$ and $A^1\Pi(v = 2)$ states, reveal that the perturbation pathways are indirect, primarily facilitated by the $e^3\Sigma^-(v = 4)$ state, and that quantum mechanical interferences via its F1e and F3e components occur.
item.dc:creator: Stanis{\l}aw Ryzner, Robert W. Field, Wim Ubachs, Alan N. Heays, Asen Pashov, Patryk Jasik, J\'ozef E. Sienkiewicz, Nelson de Oliveira, Kin F. Lai, Marzena I. Malicka, Aleksandra Stasik, Wojciech Szajna, Izabela Piotrowska, Rafa{\l} Hakalla

item.title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
item.description: arXiv:2611.32851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyao Wang, Lun Song, Yakun Zeng, Xingao Gong, Rui Shi, Mao Su

item.title: Fast and Accurate Boys Function Evaluation Using Nonuniform Gridded Taylor Expansions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient Boys function evaluation is important for Gaussian integral calculations on both central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs). Gridded Taylor expansion provides a simple evaluation procedure, but a uniformly spaced reference table requires substantial storage over a wide argument range. We address this limitation using a nonuniform grid whose spacing increases with the argument. For large arguments, we introduce a normalized auxiliary function whose scaling and derivative properties allow it to be evaluated using the same Taylor procedure as the main-domain Boys functions. The main-domain and large-argument reference tables are constructed jointly, with polynomial degrees and grid parameters selected under accuracy and storage constraints. Low-part corrections to the reference values are included to improve the accuracy of the Taylor evaluation. The resulting method is implemented in the Fast and Accurate BOys (FABO) library and evaluated in QUICK and NWChem-Simint. FABO gives the smallest maximum and mean errors among the tested implementations for all three reported error measures, with the largest sampled error being approximately 1.067 units in the last place (ULPs). In application benchmarks, FABO reduces the Fock-build time relative to the original Boys evaluators in both applications and is competitive with the other tested implementations.
item.dc:creator: Longxiang Yan, Wei Wu, Peifeng Su

item.title: Spin-adapted state preparation for quantum chemistry
item.description: arXiv:2611.30014v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum phase estimation for strongly-correlated molecules requires an initial state of high overlap with the true ground state, and preparing one is a significant fault-tolerant cost. Matrix product states (MPS) produced by the density matrix renormalisation group (DMRG) are a leading choice, yet existing circuits treat their tensors as dense or do not use the full symmetries present in molecular electronic Hamiltonians. In quantum chemistry, DMRG also exploits total spin, a non-abelian symmetry, storing one amplitude per spin multiplet instead of one per state. We show that the reduced tensors of such a spin-adapted MPS, labelled by the steps of the unitary group approach, form an abelian-symmetric MPS, which existing block-sparse preparation protocols can load at a cost set by the multiplet count. One state-independent rotation per site, determined by a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient, then returns the state to the occupation basis. We provide resource estimates for our circuits on singlet ground states of active space models of iron-sulphur clusters, finding improvements in Toffoli count up to $135\times$ compared to dense methods and $4.9\times$ compared to block-sparse methods applied to the same states, with up to $3.7\times$ fewer ancilla qubits required.
item.dc:creator: Matthew L. Sims-Goh, Fredrik Hasselgren, Hamza Jnane

item.title: What time is it in Assembly Space? Cronin and Walker's "The Physics of Causation" fails elementary dimensional analysis (Comment on arXiv:2601.00515)
item.description: arXiv:2611.31339v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cronin and Walker claim that causation is quantified by an ``assembly index'', a count of the steps needed to build an object. Remarkably, they equate ``continuous time (as measured by clocks)'' to a multiple of the index, which is a dimensionless number. Their argument treats one parameter as simultaneously a rate, a time interval, and a pure number, and provides no timescale to convert index to clock time. This dimensional incoherence betrays, at best, an ill-conceived and ill-formed theory, and fatally undermines two central claims. First, the exponential weighting at the heart of what they call the assembly equation can be obtained only by supplying a timescale, which they never do, or by recasting clock time as a dimensionless count of assembly steps. In the latter case, their ``derivation'' trivially reduces to Bernoulli's seventeenth-century compound-interest limit. Second, lacking rates or energy scales, their account cannot predict how quickly, or under what conditions, anything forms, and yet formation ``in finite time'' is their criterion for distinguishing spontaneous from ``selected'' objects. Assembly theory is thus incapable of addressing causation.
item.dc:creator: Philip Moriarty

item.title: H$_3^+$ forbidden rotational lines in a planetary nebula: JWST/MIRI detection in the Ring Nebula and ionization by the central star
item.description: arXiv:2611.31633v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report the detection of the forbidden pure rotational spectrum of H$_3^+$ in the Ring Nebula (NGC 6720), to our knowledge the first detection of H$_3^+$ in a planetary nebula. In JWST/MIRI spectra obtained toward the inner edge of the main ring, 0.1 pc in projection from the central star, the $(J,K) = (5,0)\to(4,3)$ line at 16.325 $\mu$m is detected at $32\sigma$, along with nine further unblended lines. The H$_3^+$ emission spatially follows the H$_2$ emission, whose rotational lines show warm (660 K) and hot (1700 K) components. A statistical-equilibrium model at these temperatures reproduces the subthermal H$_3^+$ line pattern, with much of the emission arising in the hot H$_2$. The emission requires an H$_2$ ionization rate of $\sim 3\times 10^{-12}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ in the hot H$_2$ for an electron fraction of $2\times 10^{-4}$. The rate is $\sim 2\times 10^4$ times the cosmic-ray ionization rate in diffuse clouds. The extreme-ultraviolet and soft X-ray radiation (54-300 eV) of the 135 kK central star supplies this rate if the hot H$_2$ lies within an H-nucleus column density of (4-8)$\times 10^{19}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$ of the ionization front of the dense globules. Static photoionization models, however, place the H$_2$ in gas too cold to excite the H$_3^+$ lines. The warm molecular gas and its H$_3^+$ thus suggest dynamical effects, most plausibly the advection of H$_2$ through a photoevaporation front into gas heated by the star. H$_3^+$ provides a new probe of the photoionization of molecular gas by very hot stars.
item.dc:creator: David A. Neufeld (JHU), Paule Sonnentrucker (STScI, ESA), Joel D. Green (STScI)

item.title: Electron versus positron impact ionization of inner shells of heavy atoms: distortion, exchange and relativistic effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.31716v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Triple differential cross sections are presented for electron and positron impact ionization of the K shells of Cu, Ag, Au and U and the L shells of Ag. Relativistic effects are important throughout. For positrons the recoil maximum is suppressed and the recoil-region spin asymmetry changes sign; for the $2s$ shell the binary peak changes. In symmetric geometry, where theory reproduces the measured absolute electron cross section, the positron peak lies on the other side of zero recoil. Measurements would test relativistic ionization theory in a regime that electron experiments cannot reach.
item.dc:creator: Colm T. Whelan

item.title: Periodic and quasiperiodic structures produced by microphase separation in one-component simple liquids with competing interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32273v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Competing interactions can generate frustration which suppresses macroscopic-scale phase separation, superseding it with separation patterns on the microscopic scale. This phenomenon, referred to as microphase separation, produces thermodynamically stable mesoscopic-scale periodic patterns in systems of different physical nature. The studies of this effect follow two paradigms. First, in block copolymers, the macroscopic-scale separation of chemically distinct components is prevented by the covalent bonds between them. In the other, the microscopic-scale separation is produced in simple single-component liquids by the competition between a short-range attraction and a long-range repulsion (SALR) in the pair potential, the separation occurring between a dense phase and a gas. The interest in the simple liquid models with SALR interaction was inspired by the apparent universality of the modulated structures generated by competing interactions in different systems. Simple particle models are tractable by theory and thereby make it possible to discern the microscopic mechanisms of pattern formation; particle-based simulations give access to systems beyond the reach of experiments. In this Perspective we review the recent advances in the molecular-dynamics simulation of microphase separation in single-component simple liquids using SALR potentials. We show that these simulations reproduce the mesophases typical of block copolymers and liquid crystals, which demonstrates that the complexity of the constituent particles of real liquids is not a necessary condition for their formation, and that they produce novel periodic morphologies of both conceptual interest and technological relevance; we discuss how simulated mesophases can serve as templates for metamaterials whose properties are governed by topology.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Agosta, Alfredo Metere, Mikhail Dzugutov

item.title: X-ray induced structural and dynamical changes in supramolecular polymer networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.32349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beam-induced effects are key considerations in X-ray scattering studies of soft matter. Because these experiments typically aim to probe the unperturbed system, the structural and dynamic changes induced by the beam often remain underexplored. In the study at hand, the influence of X-rays on metallo-supramolecular tetra-arm poly(ethylene glycol) (tetra-PEG) networks is studied in dependence of the dose rate. Based on their transient interlinkage, such materials have the ability to reconnect and self-heal mechanical damage. Here, wide- and small-angle X-ray Scattering were employed to understand the effect of X-rays on the micro- and mesoscale structure of such polymer networks. Dynamical effects were probed using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy. A restructuring of the polymer chains in the network is observed over several length scales, indicating a pre-crystallization step induced by the ionizing radiation, accompanied by expulsion of water from the network. In conjunction, a complex dynamical behavior is observed, consisting of an initial fast process, followed by an overall slow-down during the restructuring process. The two-time correlation functions exhibit an oscillatory behavior related to the development of multiple dynamic populations in the polymer network.
item.dc:creator: Niels C. Gie{\ss}elmann, Yasothaa Thavayogarajah, Tobias Eklund, Louisa E. Kraft, Isabell Zick, Yizhi Liu, Fiona Berner, Felix Lehmk\"uhler, Fabian Westermeier, Mostafa Ahmadi, Sebastian Seiffert, Katrin Amann-Winkel

item.title: Neutron Spectroscopy Transformed: Deuterated ZIF-8 and Machine-Learned Potentials Catch Nitrogen Threading Its Gates
item.description: arXiv:2611.32739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report a step change in what inelastic neutron scattering (INS) can reveal, by combining machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with deliberate deuteration of the sample. INS's prowess in charting framework and guest motions within porous materials during in situ dosing has historically had one caveat: costly density-functional-theory calculations are a major bottleneck in the speed and depth of analysis. We show that rapid frontier MLIPs remove this bottleneck on both counts, keeping pace with the experiment while bringing a new level of insight. Deuterating the linkers of ZIF-8 pries apart bands that overlap in the hydrogenous framework, and we test four MLIPs against eight stages of nitrogen dosing at 77 K. On loading, a previously unobserved band appears at 270 cm^-1 and grows gradually through the dosing series. The simulations trace it to single N2 molecules threaded end-on through four-ring windows, each turning its ring of linkers and propping the window open, and unbiased dynamics catch molecules threading into the windows on their own, finding a free-energy trap that crowding stabilizes. This is the first vibrational signature of the threaded state and, crucially, its intensity directly counts the threading over the slow, macroscopic timescale of gas uptake, in situ. More broadly, the simulations explain how each framework band responds to its guests, establishing MLIP-assisted inelastic neutron scattering as a route to mechanism, not just assignment.
item.dc:creator: Jeff Armstrong, Hamish Cavaye, Pankaj Sharma, Matthew E. Potter

item.title: Giant Nonequilibrium Fluctuations at a Reactive Surface
item.description: arXiv:2606.18760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate whether giant fluctuations in a gas can induce corresponding fluctuations on a reactive surface in contact with the gas. Numerical simulations of a minimal heterogeneous catalytic reactor demonstrate that such fluctuations indeed emerge on the surface, with spatial correlations extending over micrometer scales. These fluctuations originate from the dependence of the adsorption rate on the reactant partial pressure. As a result, the surface-coverage structure factor mirrors that of the partial pressure, exhibiting similar enhancement and roll-off behavior across wave numbers.
item.dc:creator: Hyun Tae Jung, Hyungjun Kim, Alejandro L. Garcia, Andrew J. Nonaka, John B. Bell, Ishan Srivastava, Changho Kim

item.title: PyCC: A Reference Quantum Chemistry Python Package for Education, Validation, and Rapid Prototyping
item.description: arXiv:2610.04107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: PyCC is a Python-based quantum chemistry package that emphasizes coupled cluster and related methods. Developed over the last five years, PyCC's purpose is to provide a clear reference implementation that will serve as a validation suite for production code, a platform for rapid prototyping and testing of new methods, and an educational resource for newcomers to the field. The package covers both closed- and open-shell single-determinant references in spatial- and spin-orbital formulations for the coupled cluster hierarchy through triples-including methods such as CC3, as well as for MP2 and CI methods. PyCC provides a broad range of molecular properties such as analytic first and second energy derivatives including gradients, Hessians, polarizabilities and atomic polar tensors, as well as non-energy-derivative properties, such as velocity-gauge atomic polar tensors and diagonal Born-Oppenheimer corrections, plus dynamic linear response functions, and excitation energies. The package includes a number of unique capabilities, such as real-time CC propagation (up through CC3), atomic axial tensors for simulating vibrational circular dichroism spectra at the MP2, CID, CISD, and CCSD levels, and local correlation methods including perturbation-aware correlation domains. The code is designed around a shared Wavefunction base and a method-agnostic derivative layer that enables a new method to inherit the full energy-derivative property set once it supplies its reduced densities and their first-order responses. PyCC is fully open source and available on GitHub under the BSD 3-clause license.
item.dc:creator: T. Daniel Crawford, Benjamin G. Peyton, Zhe Wang, Aparna Krishnan, Brendan M. Shumberger, Jose Madriaga, Joshua Atta-Kumi, Aaron De Clercq, Ritvik Prabhu

item.title: Adding Temperature to the Adiabatic Connection: Hybrid Functionals for Static and Dynamic Correlation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22284v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Capturing static and dynamic electron correlation simultaneously at manageable computational cost remains a key challenge in electronic structure theory. Motivated by the recurring role of effective temperature in self-consistent field methods we extend the adiabatic connection mechanism from density functional theory (DFT) to include a temperature dimension. The formalism unifies established hybrid functionals with information-density matrix functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation DFT, clarifying their theoretical basis and the respective prescriptions for the temperature parameter. It further gives rise to thermally enhanced hybrid functionals, in which static correlation is captured via fractional occupations generated by an effective "correlation temperature" within thermal Hartree-Fock, while dynamic correlation is described by established density functional approximations. We assess the performance of several thermally enhanced hybrids for different cases where i-DMFT was previously shown to fail. Furthermore, we discuss and test different schemes for determining the correlation temperature and investigate the accuracy of different such choices for a benchmark set of different organic molecules. The results clarify the achievable balance of accuracy, generality, and efficiency, establishing thermally enhanced hybrids as a systematic route toward low-cost treatment of both correlation types.
item.dc:creator: Florian Matz, Paul G. Graf, Markus Penz, Christian Schilling

item.title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.06533v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this manuscript, we outline a computational strategy to leverage (vendor-)optimized implementations of the Ozaki schemes I and II for floating-point emulation as part of an implementation of the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) pattern for tensor contractions, and assess its potential to accelerate two of the most expensive tensor contractions appearing in relativistic coupled cluster theory in high-end accelerators such as the NVIDIA Blackwell B200 system, in which there is a strong differential in the performance of computations for double and lower precision datatypes. Our results indicate that this emulation-based TTGT strategy can provide significant speedups compared to runs without emulation, and can be competitive with state-of-the-art, (vendor-)optimized tensor contraction libraries using native double precision as compute datatype. More importantly, our scheme provides a path towards easily allowing users to tune the desired accuracy in the tensor contraction steps, including cases where precision between single and double is sufficient for the application.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Le, Ryan Benazzouk, Jan Brandejs, Andre Severo Pereira Gomes

item.title: Energy-Guided Generative Modeling for Low-Energy Molecular Structure Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2512.22597v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exploring molecular energy landscapes and identifying ground-state conformations are central challenges in computational chemistry. However, generating diverse low-energy conformers from molecular graphs remains expensive with traditional physics-based pipelines. Existing learning-based approaches remain fragmented: generative models capture conformational diversity but often lack reliable energy calibration, whereas deterministic predictors focus on a single structure and fail to represent ensemble variability. Here we introduce EnFlow, to our knowledge, the first energy-guided generative framework that couples flow-based conformer generation with explicit energy landscape modeling for joint conformational ensemble generation and ground-state identification. By integrating generative dynamics with a learned energy model, EnFlow guides sampling toward low-energy regions of the conformational landscape, improving structural fidelity under extremely few sampling steps while enabling energy-based ranking of generated conformations. Experiments on GEOM-QM9 and GEOM-Drugs show that EnFlow achieves strong performance in conformer generation and ground-state identification while requiring only 1-2 ordinary differential equation (ODE) sampling steps. Single-point GFN2-xTB evaluations further show that the learned energy scores preserve physically meaningful energetic rankings of generated conformations. These results support explicit energy landscape modeling as an effective strategy for low-energy molecular structure discovery through joint modeling of conformational ensembles and their associated energies.
item.dc:creator: Guikun Xu, Xiaohan Yi, Ziqiao Meng, Peilin Zhao, Yatao Bian

item.title: Light-Matter Interactions Beyond the Electric Dipole Approximation in Extended Systems Without Multipole Expansion
item.description: arXiv:2603.10271v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a general theoretical framework to capture light-matter interactions beyond the electric-dipole approximation, applicable to extended materials interacting with spatially structured electric fields without truncation at finite multipolar order. The approach is based on the Power-Zienau-Woolley (PZW) Hamiltonian for light-matter interactions and a representation of the material Hamiltonian in a basis of maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs). We utilize this novel approach to clarify the limitations of the ubiquitous dipole approximation. We consider electric fields with both uniform and non-uniform intensity profiles and a range of ratios of system size to the wavelength of light. We identify the precise conditions under which the dipole approximation breaks down, leading to significant errors in the light-induced dynamics. Contrary to conventional belief, we find that the dipole approximation is robust for uniformly illuminated 1D or 2D materials if light propagates perpendicular to the material. For 3D materials or non-perpendicular illumination, the dipole approximation starts to break down when the wavelength of light becomes comparable to the system size. Furthermore, the dipole approximation fails to capture the light-matter interaction when the material is illuminated partially or non-uniformly. For slowly varying field intensities this failure can be corrected by the finite-order multipolar corrections. However, for fields that vary substantially over the system size, correcting via finite order multipolar terms becomes computationally impractical. In contrast, our approach captures the beyond-dipole light-matter interactions at a computational cost of a standard dipole calculation. This efficiency paves the way for accurate first-principles simulations of spatially-structured light-matter dynamics in nanoscale devices, quantum materials, and interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Rishabh Dora, Roman Korol, Vishal Tiwari, Rahul Chourasiya, Ignacio Franco

item.title: Poincar\'e sphere representation of spin-driven polarization encoding in two-dimensional perovskite light sources
item.description: arXiv:2605.28695v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Nonlinear optical light sources enable the generation of photons with polarization states that are intrinsically determined by underlying material dynamics, rather than imposed through external modulation. Here, we investigate how four-wave-mixing signal fields emitted by a representative two-dimensional perovskite system can be leveraged for polarization-encoded quantum communication. The experimentally reconstructed signal field is represented by Stokes-vector trajectories on the Poincar\'e sphere to establish a predictive framework that connects the optical response to practical figures of merit for spin-driven semiconductor light sources. Applied to a model quantum communication scheme in the weak coherent-state regime, this representation quantifies the resolution of the polarization states generated at two pump-probe delays, thereby enabling estimation of the number of detected photons per decoded bit. In addition, a microscopic model connects the signal-field ellipticity to spin relaxation within the exciton fine structure, revealing that interference between resonantly enhanced optical transitions governs the accessible polarization states. The analysis suggests that modest stabilization of the lowest-energy biexciton could substantially improve polarization-encoding performance, offering a route toward materials optimization. More broadly, these results motivate closer integration of nonlinear spectroscopy, semiconductor materials, and quantum information science in the development of novel light sources for quantum communication.
item.dc:creator: Zijian Gan, Shuyue Feng, Camryn J. Gloor, Wei You, Andrew M. Moran

item.title: Microphase Separation and Ionic Aggregation in Oppositely Charged End-Functionalized Polymer Blends
item.description: arXiv:2610.24361v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using an ion-correlation-augmented self-consistent field theory (IC-SCFT), we study the phase behavior of binary blends of A and B polymers carrying single end groups of opposite charge. Under the low dielectric conditions typical for organic polymer melts, strong ion correlations drive association of multiple chain ends, leading to emergent multichain architectures that go beyond a simple ion-paired diblock copolymer picture previously used to interpret recent experiments. At moderate to strong polymer segregation, the resulting phase diagram differs considerably from this effective-diblock prediction: ion clustering broadens the lamellar and cylindrical windows while suppressing the network phases, the reverse of the trend for end-charged diblock copolymers. At weak segregation, the two polymers remain miscible even as ion clustering persists, and decreasing chain length drives the clusters themselves through a sphere-to-cylinder-to-lamella shape transition, connecting continuously to the aggregation behavior of classical terminally charged ionomers in the limit when one of the polymer species shrinks to just the charged end. These results reveal that ion clustering - beyond simple pairwise bonding - shapes the self-assembly of end-charged polymer blends.
item.dc:creator: Chao Duan, Zhen-Gang Wang
